name: Bee hummingbird
height: A few centimetres tall
place: Cuba and the Isla de la Juventud
fact: Birds ARE dinosaurs: the living branch of the theropods, T. rex's group. At about two grams, this is the smallest living bird, and so the smallest known dinosaur.
compare: about as long as a credit card is tall (5.4 cm)

name: Anchiornis
height: Wingspan of the largest specimens ≈57 cm
place: Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China
diet: Carnivore (gut pellets hold lizard bones and fish scales)
fact: In 2010, fossil pigment sacs revealed its colours: grey-black body, reddish crown, and black-tipped white wing feathers. It was the first dinosaur coloured head to toe.
compare: a little longer than a 30 cm ruler

name: Archaeopteryx
height: Wingspan up to ≈70 cm
place: Solnhofen limestones, Bavaria, Germany
fact: Its first skeleton was found in 1861, two years after Darwin's 'Origin of Species': feathered wings, plus teeth, claws and a bony tail. Fourteen are known.
compare: magpie-sized; the biggest were about as big as a raven

name: Microraptor
height: Wingspan ≈0.9–1 m, with feathered wings on arms AND legs
place: Jiufotang Formation, Liaoning, China
diet: Carnivore (gut contents: a bird, a mammal's foot, fish, a lizard)
fact: Its fossil feathers held narrow, stacked pigment sacs like a starling's. In 2012, scientists concluded that this four-winged dinosaur was glossy, iridescent black.
compare: four-winged and about as long as an adult's arm

sources.label: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Microraptor

name: Eoraptor
length: ≈1.2–1.3 m (Sereno et al. 2013); NHM gives up to 1.7 m
height: Small and light: thigh bone only ≈15 cm long
place: Ischigualasto Formation, 'Valley of the Moon', San Juan, Argentina
fact: One of the earliest dinosaurs, about 230 million years old. First called a meat-eating theropod, it is now usually placed near the start of the sauropod line.
compare: about as long as a 7-year-old is tall, and as heavy as a beagle

sources.label: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Eoraptor

name: Compsognathus
length: 1.25–1.4 m (large French adult); German specimen 0.7–0.9 m (juvenile)
height: ≈29 cm at the hips (French specimen)
place: Bavaria, Germany, and Canjuers, southern France
fact: Both known skeletons have lizards in their bellies. The German one tore its lizard apart and swallowed it; in 2017 that lizard became a new species, Schoenesmahl dyspepsia.
compare: about as heavy as a house cat

name: Velociraptor
height: ≈0.5 m at the hips
place: Gobi Desert: Djadokhta Formation, Mongolia; Inner Mongolia, China
fact: In 2007, quill knobs, the anchors for big wing feathers, were reported on a Velociraptor forearm. It was feathered, with hips only knee-high to a human.
compare: about as heavy as a coyote

name: Protoceratops
height: ≈0.6 m at the hips (approximate)
mass: ≈60–105 kg (Campione & Evans 2020); some older figures much higher
place: Gobi Desert: Mongolia and Inner Mongolia, China
fact: Protoceratops laid soft, leathery eggs like a turtle's. A 2020 study concluded that the first dinosaur eggs were soft, and hard shells evolved at least three times.
compare: about the size of a sheep

sources.label: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Protoceratops
Norell et al. 2020, Nature (The first dinosaur egg was soft)

name: Coelophysis
height: a little over 1 m at the hips
place: Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, USA (Chinle Formation)
fact: In January 1998 a Coelophysis skull rode Space Shuttle Endeavour (STS-89) to the Mir space station. It was only the second dinosaur in space, after Maiasaura.
compare: as long as a small car, but only as heavy as a 7-year-old

name: Deinonychus
height: ≈0.87 m at the hips
mass: ≈60–73 kg (Paul); up to ≈100 kg (Campione et al.)
period: Early Cretaceous (Aptian–Albian), possibly into the Cenomanian
place: Montana, Wyoming and Oklahoma, USA (Cloverly and Antlers formations)
fact: John Ostrom described this agile hunter, with its 12 cm sickle claw, in 1969. That work sparked the 'Dinosaur Renaissance': dinosaurs were active, bird-like animals, not sluggish lizards.
compare: as long as a small car, and about as heavy as an adult human

name: Pachycephalosaurus
length: ≈3–4.5 m (estimates vary: known mostly from skulls)
height: Body poorly known; skull roof up to ≈22–25 cm thick
place: Montana, South Dakota and Wyoming (USA); Alberta (Canada)
diet: Herbivore (diet uncertain; possibly some other foods)
fact: A 2013 study found healed bone infections on 22% of pachycephalosaur domes, matching head-to-head combat. Flat-headed individuals showed none.
compare: as long as a car, and as heavy as a grand piano

sources.label: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Pachycephalosaurus
Peterson, Dischler & Longrich 2013, PLoS ONE (dome lesions)

name: Ankylosaurus
height: ≈1.4–1.7 m at the hips (Carpenter 2004)
place: Montana and Wyoming (USA); Alberta and Saskatchewan (Canada)
fact: Its tail club, up to 57 cm wide, was made of armour plates on fused tail vertebrae. A 2009 study found adult clubs could break bone.
compare: longer than a pickup truck, and as heavy as an elephant

name: Dilophosaurus
height: ≈1.4–1.75 m at the hips
place: Kayenta Formation, northern Arizona, USA (Navajo Nation)
fact: A 2020 redescription found air sacs reaching into its paired head crests, which were probably sheathed in keratin. Its snout was also far more robust than once thought.
compare: longer than a minibus, but a bit lighter than a horse

name: Triceratops
height: ≈2.3–3 m tall (mounted specimens 'Kelsey' and 'Big John')
place: Western North America (Wyoming, Montana, the Dakotas, Colorado, Alberta, Saskatchewan)
fact: The 'Lane' specimen preserves large patches of skin texture, with scales more than 10 cm across. Triceratops wore a coat of big, pebbly scales.
compare: heavier than an African elephant

name: Allosaurus
height: roughly 2.5–3 m at the hips (approximate)
place: Morrison Formation, western USA; also Portugal
fact: One Allosaurus tail bone has a partly healed puncture that fits a Stegosaurus tail spike exactly. The predator survived this Jurassic duel, at least for a while.
compare: as long as two cars nose to tail, and about as heavy as a white rhino

name: Stegosaurus
length: ≈6.5–7 m typical; large individuals 7.5–9 m (shown: 9 m)
height: 'Sophie' specimen: 2.9 m tall to the tips of its plates
place: Morrison Formation (Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, USA); also Portugal
fact: Stegosaurus weighed over 4.5 tonnes, but its brain was no heavier than about 80 grams. That was proportionally one of the smallest brains of any dinosaur.
compare: as heavy as an elephant

sources.label: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Stegosaurus

name: Parasaurolophus
height: Could browse up to ≈4 m high; skull with crest ≈1.6 m long
place: Alberta (Canada); New Mexico and Utah (USA)
fact: Its hollow crest held looping air tubes. A 1990s computer model of a crested skull found it resonated at about 30 hertz, a deep, low call.
compare: about as long as a school bus

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
height: 3.66–3.96 m at the hips (Sue)
place: Western North America (Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming, Alberta, Saskatchewan…)
fact: A 2023 study of tooth enamel and tooth size concluded that T. rex probably had lizard-like lips. They would have covered its teeth when its mouth was closed.
compare: about as long as a city bus

sources.label: Hutchinson et al. 2011, PLoS ONE (body mass)

name: Spinosaurus
length: ≈14 m (Sereno et al. 2022); some estimates 15+ m
height: Sail spines at least 1.65 m tall; hind leg ≈2.9 m long
place: Egypt (Bahariya Formation) and Morocco (Kem Kem beds)
fact: In 2020, a nearly complete tail revealed tall spines forming a fin-like paddle, and robot tests suggested it could swim. Others argue it waded like a giant heron.
compare: longer than a city bus

sources.label: Sereno et al. 2022, eLife (size and wading)

name: Shantungosaurus
height: Its skull alone was ≈1.63 m long
place: Wangshi Group, Zhucheng, Shandong, China
fact: It was the largest known duck-billed dinosaur. Behind its toothless beak, its jaws were packed with about 1,500 small grinding teeth.
compare: longer than a city bus, and as heavy as two or three elephants

sources.label: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Shantungosaurus

name: Brachiosaurus
height: ≈9.4 m (Foster) to 12–13 m (Paul) tall; head over 9 m off the ground
place: Morrison Formation, western USA (holotype near Fruita, Colorado)
fact: The famous giant skeleton in Berlin is not Brachiosaurus. It is Giraffatitan from Tanzania, given its own genus in 2009 after Taylor found 26 differences.
compare: its head could peer into a third-floor window

name: Diplodocus
height: Hips well above an adult's head; tail ≈55% of its length
place: Morrison Formation, western USA ('Dippy' came from Wyoming)
fact: Between 1905 and 1928, Andrew Carnegie sent casts of 'Dippy' to museums from London to Mexico City. It has been displayed in more places than any other sauropod.
compare: longer than a tennis court (23.8 m)

name: Patagotitan
length: ≈31–37 m (31 m, Paul; 37 m, original description)
height: The Field Museum cast 'Máximo' stands 8.5 m (28 ft) tall at the head
place: Cerro Barcino Formation, Chubut, Patagonia, Argentina
fact: Bones of at least six young adults were found at one ranch site. First reported at 69–77 tonnes, it was re-weighed in 2020 at about 57 tonnes.
compare: about as long as a Boeing 737 airliner

name: Argentinosaurus
height: ≈7.3 m at the shoulder (Sellers et al. 2013)
place: Huincul Formation, Neuquén Province, Patagonia, Argentina
fact: It is known only from fragments, but one back vertebra is about 1.59 m tall. It is a top contender for the heaviest land animal ever.
compare: about as long as a blue whale, and as heavy as about 12 elephants

sources.label: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Argentinosaurus
Maniel et al. 2026, Gondwana Research (Albian U-Pb ages, Huincul Fm.)

note: Dating is debated: traditionally ≈96–93 million years ago (Cenomanian–Turonian), but a 2026 U-Pb study re-dates its rocks to ≈106 million years ago.

name: The Chicxulub impactor
diameter: ≈10 km (standard estimate; model values span ≈10–20 km depending on assumed speed and density)
impact_date: ≈66.04 million years ago: 66.043 ± 0.011 Ma (± 0.043 Ma including systematic error; Renne et al. 2013). A 2018 Gorgonilla Island date gives 66.051 ± 0.031 Ma.
impact_speed: ≈20 km/s (the most probable speed modelled; models span ≈12–20 km/s)
impact_angle: steep, ≈45–60° from horizontal, arriving from the north-east
crater: ≈180–200 km across (Chicxulub crater, buried ≈1 km deep)
location: Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico (centre near Chicxulub Pueblo; 21°24′N 89°30′W)
energy: ≈10²³–10²⁴ J in most estimates (some up to 10²⁵ J)
energy_mt: ≈100 million megatons of TNT (≈4 × 10²³ J); published estimates run from tens of millions to billions of megatons
hiroshima: ≈7–10 billion Hiroshima-size bombs. UT Austin gives 'the equivalent power of 10 billion atomic bombs of the size used in World War II'; 100 million Mt ÷ 15 kt ≈ 6.7 billion
extinction: ≈75% of plant and animal species (≈76% in During et al. 2022)
aftermath: Dust, soot and sulfur blocked out the Sun. Within days, fine dust had wrapped the whole planet in an impact winter.
Photosynthesis on land and in the sea shut down for almost two years.
Models suggest sub-freezing temperatures for 3–16 years and over 30 years of recovery. Sea temperatures plunged for months to decades.
Survivors were mostly small: birds, rat-sized mammals, crocodilians (about half), turtles (over 80%), and some lizards and snakes.
survivors: The only dinosaurs to survive were birds. Every non-avian dinosaur died out, but one branch of small feathered theropods came through, and today they are all around us.
survivors_short: Birds are living dinosaurs: the only dinosaur branch to survive the impact, they now number more than 11,000 species.
finale_rows: A 10 km asteroid hit Mexico’s Yucatán at about 20 km/s
It blasted a crater 180–200 km wide, with the energy of billions of Hiroshima bombs
Dust and soot shut down photosynthesis for almost two years
About 3 in 4 species vanished. Of the dinosaurs, only the birds survived
fact: Set down at sea level, the 10 km asteroid would have stood taller than Mount Everest.

sources.label: Renne et al. 2013, Science (66.043 Ma age)
Collins et al. 2020, Nature Communications (speed and angle)
University of Texas at Austin news, 2019 (10 billion atomic bombs)
VUB press release on Senel et al. 2023, Nature Geoscience (dust, about two years without photosynthesis)
Brugger et al. 2017, Geophysical Research Letters (3–16 years sub-freezing)
During et al. 2022, Nature (≈76% of species; impact in spring)
